rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The linked stories of Mary, Zachariah, John, and Jesus show that divine creative power crosses ordinary physical limits.
rows.anchor: The two stories are also connected in 21:89–91 as well as in the Biblical account found in Luke 1:5–80

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The wording may make Zachariah himself the mercy God bestowed on his people.
rows.anchor: indicating that Zachariah himself was a mercy from God bestowed upon his people (R).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening mention of mercy fits the sūrah’s repeated use of al-Raḥmān, from the same root.
rows.anchor: namely, that God is referred to throughout as al-Raḥmān, “the Compassionate”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zachariah’s secret supplication signals sincerity; loud prayer can suggest hypocrisy or seeking human notice.
rows.anchor: That Zachariah cries out to God with a secret cry indicates his sincerity

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: A low voice is especially favored by God.
rows.anchor: this mode of supplication is particularly favored by God (IK)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Zachariah may have prayed quietly because of age and frailty or fear of his relatives.
rows.anchor: as a result of his age and frailty (Z), or because of fear of his relatives

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Zachariah was said to be between sixty and eighty-five years old.
rows.anchor: as he was said to be between sixty and eighty-five years old at this time (Z).

rows.speaker: Bḍ, Mw
rows.claim: His claim never to have been wretched in prayer means God had always answered his supplications.
rows.anchor: God had always answered his prayers (Bḍ, Mw).

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: Zachariah feared that his relatives would fail to guide the community or uphold religion after his death.
rows.anchor: he feared that his relatives would not continue to guide the religious community or uphold the religion properly after his death (Bḍ).

rows.speaker: Mw
rows.claim: The word mawālī may mean agnatic relatives who would inherit Zachariah’s position if he had no son.
rows.anchor: may refer to his agnatic relatives, who would inherit his position after him if he had no son (Mw)

rows.speaker: Mw
rows.claim: Alternatively, mawālī may mean unrelated religious scholars who might assume leadership of the Jewish community.
rows.anchor: other, unrelated religious scholars who might assume religious leadership of the Jewish community after him (Mw).

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: Walī means an heir in this context, rather than its other Qurʾānic senses of protector or friend.
rows.anchor: in this context refers to an heir, since it concerns Zachariah’s desire for a child of his own (Bḍ)

rows.speaker: Bḍ, Mw
rows.claim: The desired heir would inherit religious knowledge and authority, perhaps prophethood, rather than necessarily inheriting wealth.
rows.anchor: who could be heir to his religious knowledge and authority and perhaps to his function of prophethood (Mw)

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: A well-known ḥadīth says prophets do not leave heirs to their wealth.
rows.anchor: a well-known ḥadīth asserts that the prophets do not have heirs to their wealth (Bḍ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spiritual sense of inheritance is supported by references to the blessed House of Jacob and to the Book and Wisdom given Abraham’s house.
rows.anchor: That it is spiritual and not material inheritance that is meant here

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: A child from aged parents would be a gift from God’s Presence beyond ordinary human childbearing.
rows.anchor: nothing other than a Divine Gift (Bḍ).

rows.speaker: Mw
rows.claim: Well-pleasing means that God will approve the heir’s character and deeds.
rows.anchor: that God will be pleased with his character and deeds (Mw).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurʾānic riḍā links divine contentment with believers’ aim and with the paradisal state.
rows.anchor: the Contentment of God is what true believers strive for

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A ḥadīth says that whoever is content with God’s decree will have God’s contentment.
rows.anchor: “Whosoever is content with God’s Decree, God is content with him”

rows.speaker: R, Ṭs
rows.claim: The announcement may have come directly from God or through one or more angelic messengers.
rows.anchor: messenger (R) or messengers (Ṭs; see 3:39).

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Yaḥyā means “he lives” and may refer to Zachariah’s faith being brought to life.
rows.anchor: it may refer to John’s having been brought to life through Zachariah’s faith (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: The name may refer to John being miraculously brought to life in his mother’s womb.
rows.anchor: his having been brought to life miraculously in his mother’s womb (Bḍ).

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that God enlivened John’s heart with faith and obedience.
rows.anchor: God having enlivened his heart with faith and obedience (R).

rows.speaker: R, Ṭs
rows.claim: God’s naming John before birth is a special honor; Jesus also receives his name from God.
rows.anchor: That God Himself gives John his name is a distinct honor (R, Ṭs); Jesus is also given his name by God

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: The unprecedented name marks John’s special favor and virtue.
rows.anchor: the special favor bestowed upon John, and his virtue (Ṭs;

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The name’s uniqueness may reflect that God named John before birth, unlike children named by their parents afterward.
rows.anchor: he was named by God Himself prior to his birth, while other children are named by their parents after they are born (R).

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Shiite tradition links John’s unprecedented name and martyrdom to al-Ḥusayn’s name given by the Prophet and his martyrdom under Yazīd.
rows.anchor: whose name, according to Shiite sources, was given by the Prophet himself and also had no precedent

rows.speaker: IK, Mw
rows.claim: Zachariah’s question expresses awe at divine creative power or asks how the child will be granted given his wife’s barrenness.
rows.anchor: either to indicate his awe and wonder at God’s creative Power or because he wishes to know how

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: God’s answer means that creation requires no means for Him.
rows.anchor: God has no need of“means” by which to create (Z).

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The question may ask how the child will come about because the promise says ghulām, “boy,” not walad, “son.”
rows.anchor: walad; R), and thus did not specify that the child would be conceived and born in the normal manner.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kadhālika may be translated either “Thus shall it be” or “Thus it is.”
rows.anchor: might also be rendered “Thus it is.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creation is effortless for God: when He decrees a thing, He says “Be,” and it exists.
rows.anchor: Bringing creatures into being is easy for God

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Creating John through aged parents is no more miraculous than God’s creating Zachariah from nothing.
rows.anchor: no more miraculous than His ability to bring all things from nonexistence into existence (R, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Zachariah temporarily lost the ability to speak to people while his faculties remained sound.
rows.anchor: he was rendered temporarily incapable of speaking, though his faculties were still sound (Ṭ, Ṭs, Z).

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: His sudden inability to speak served as a sign to his people that his request had been granted.
rows.anchor: a sign for his people, who thus knew that his request had been granted (Ṭs).

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Some reports say he could still pray and praise God but could not speak to people.
rows.anchor: he continued to be capable of uttering prayers and praises to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parallel silences of Zachariah and Mary give silence spiritual significance; Sufis treat it as fitting for encounter with God.
rows.anchor: Many Sufis have indicated that silence is the only true way to communicate or express an encounter with God’s Presence

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: The miḥrāb is likely Zachariah’s personal prayer room in the Temple; the word also describes Mary’s and David’s private spaces.
rows.anchor: refers to Zachariah’s personal prayer room in the Temple (Ṭ, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In mosque architecture miḥrāb is the prayer niche marking the qiblah; its root relates to waging war.
rows.anchor: miḥrāb designates the prayer niche carved into the wall of the mosque indicating the direction of prayer

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabrisī
rows.claim: The prayer niche is so named because turning toward it in prayer spiritually wages war against Satan.
rows.anchor: one turns toward it in prayer, one is spiritually waging war against Satan

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: Zachariah communicated by gestures or by writing.
rows.anchor: he gestured to them through signs (see 3:41) or communicated to them by writing (Ṭ, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Morning-and-evening glorification may mean continual remembrance or worship at those times, whose transitions symbolize life and death.
rows.anchor: which can mean either that one should do so continuously or that one should do so at these particular times

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: The glorification may mean the regular morning and evening prayers or any form of praising God.
rows.anchor: may be a reference to the regular morning and evening prayers, during which God is praised, or to any manner of praising God (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: The address to John is understood to come immediately after his birth and commands earnest observance of the Torah.
rows.anchor: understood to have been made immediately after his birth (Q, Ṭ); it enjoins him to take the Book—that is, the Torah—with strength

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Taking the Torah with strength means seriously following it and observing its commands and prohibitions.
rows.anchor: to follow it in earnest and to observe its commands and prohibitions (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Judgment may mean understanding of scripture given in youth or John’s prophethood.
rows.anchor: refers to the understanding of the Book that God gave John as a youth or perhaps to his prophethood (R).

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: John’s precocious spiritual understanding reportedly made him uninterested in play as a child.
rows.anchor: made him disinterested in play as a child (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Ḥanān connotes gentle mercy or compassion, and its being from God’s Presence marks it as divinely bestowed.
rows.anchor: a quality of mercy that can only be bestowed by God (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Tenderness may mean God’s love for John or John himself as a tender mercy to Zachariah.
rows.anchor: Some suggest that a tenderness from Our Presence refers to the love and compassion God had for John (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Purity refers both to freedom from sin and to righteous action.
rows.anchor: John’s purity from sin as well as to his righteousness in deed (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taqwā is reverence.
rows.anchor: For the quality of“reverence” (

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: John’s dutifulness toward his parents means obedience and love.
rows.anchor: that is, obedient and loving (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: John was gentle and humble toward God and his parents, rather than domineering or rebellious.
rows.anchor: he was gentle and humble by nature (R) toward both God and his parents (Ṭ),

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says gentleness and humility are characteristic of all believers.
rows.anchor: which al-Rāzī asserts is a characteristic of all believers.

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Peace at John’s birth means protection from Satan; at death, exemption from grave trials.
rows.anchor: protection for him against the evil promptings of Satan (R, Ṭ); the blessing upon him the day he dies indicates that he is exempt from the trials of the grave

rows.speaker: Ṭ, R
rows.claim: Peace when John is raised means he will avoid resurrection dread or punishment.
rows.anchor: he will not suffer the fear and dread that will overcome others on the Day of Resurrection (Ṭ) or experience any punishment (R, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mary, daughter of ʿImrān, came from a pure noble Davidic family; her birth and dedication are recounted elsewhere.
rows.anchor: was reported to hail from a pure and noble family of the Davidic line

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mary’s purity and her mother’s prayer for protection from Satan are linked to several Qurʾānic passages.
rows.anchor: where her mother’s prayer that God will protect her from Satan is considered to have been granted

rows.speaker: Rūzbihān al-Baqlī
rows.claim: Rūzbihān says Mary’s very substance was the holy, unadulterated primordial human mold.
rows.anchor: Mary’s very substance was the holy, unadulterated fiṭrah, or the primordial human mold itself.

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: Mary withdrew to devote herself to solitary worship.
rows.anchor: Mary withdrew from her family in order to devote herself to solitary worship (R, Z).

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: The eastern place may be east of the Temple sanctuary.
rows.anchor: area “east” of the Temple sanctuary (IK,Ṭ, Z)

rows.speaker: JJ, Z
rows.claim: Alternatively, it may be east of Mary’s home.
rows.anchor: or east of her home (JJ, Z).

rows.speaker: IK, R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some say she withdrew after menstruation began.
rows.anchor: perhaps she withdrew there after the onset of menstruation (IK, R, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: Others say she withdrew to purify herself after menstruation.
rows.anchor: or to purify herself afterward (R, Z)

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: Another account says she miraculously escaped her locked prayer room to seek solitude near the Temple.
rows.anchor: she miraculously escaped her locked prayer room in order to seek solitude on a hillside or mountainous area near the Temple (R, Z).

rows.speaker: Rb, Aj
rows.claim: A spiritual reading makes her family symbolize existent worldly beings and the east a realm of Spirit; worldly withdrawal enables remembrance of God.
rows.anchor: one cannot encounter the spiritual dimension of reality until one withdraws from all worldly things that distract one from the remembrance of God

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: The veil may have been a curtain or wall shielding Mary, perhaps while she purified herself.
rows.anchor: a curtain or wall that shielded her from view (Ṭ, Z), perhaps while she was purifying herself (R).

rows.speaker: IK, R, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Most commentators identify Our Spirit as Gabriel, also called the Holy Spirit and Trustworthy Spirit.
rows.anchor: Our Spirit is considered by most to be the Archangel Gabriel

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Gabriel may be called Spirit because religion is revived through him, as spirit is associated with life.
rows.anchor: perhaps because religion is “revived” through him (Z), as spirit is also associated strongly with the giving of life

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: The angel appeared as a beautiful, radiant, proportioned, blemish-free young man, perhaps to avoid frightening Mary.
rows.anchor: a young, beardless man, beautiful and radiant in appearance, perfectly proportioned (Ṭ, Z)

rows.speaker: Ubayy ibn Kaʿb
rows.claim: Ubayy interpreted both the Spirit and the perfect man as references to Jesus’ spirit.
rows.anchor: considered the Spirit and the perfect man references to the spirit of Jesus

rows.speaker: R, Ṭs
rows.claim: A similar interpretation identifies the Spirit and man with Jesus but is not attributed to Ubayy.
rows.anchor: for a similar interpretation that is not attributed to Ubayy ibn Kaʿb

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: Mary was afraid because the unfamiliar man’s intentions were unknown to her.
rows.anchor: she is afraid, since he appeared as an unfamiliar man of whose intentions she was unsure (IK, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mary seeks refuge in God, addressed in this sūrah as al-Raḥmān.
rows.anchor: the Name al-Raḥmān (“the Compassionate”).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The refuge formula appears in Sūrahs 113–114 and is used in danger and before ablutions, prayer, or recitation.
rows.anchor: commonly uttered by Muslims in the face of great danger or evil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rasūl can denote either an angelic or a prophetic messenger.
rows.anchor: which can refer to angelic as well as prophetic messengers

rows.speaker: Bḍ, R, Z
rows.claim: Gabriel may cause conception by breathing into Mary’s sleeve or clothes.
rows.anchor: to be the cause of her conceiving a son by breathing into her sleeve or clothing

rows.speaker: Q, R, Z
rows.claim: Alternatively, Gabriel may simply announce that Mary will conceive.
rows.anchor: or else simply to bring her the news that she will conceive such a son

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: Zakī means pure from sin or fault; it may also imply growth in purity from infancy to manhood.
rows.anchor: which also relates to the concept of growth

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: Mary asks by what means conception will occur, not from doubt about the angel’s message.
rows.anchor: understood to be an inquiry as to how the conception of the child would come about

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Her denial of being touched means no normal marital intercourse; denying unchastity means innocence of illicit sex.
rows.anchor: she had not engaged in normal sexual relations through marriage, while her statement that she had not been unchaste refers to her innocence of all illicit sexual relations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A minority regard Mary as a prophet; most do not.
rows.anchor: a minority of Islamic scholars have considered Mary a female prophet

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Some take Jesus’ conception as proof that evidentiary miracles may be granted to nonprophets.
rows.anchor: may also be given to those who are not prophets

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Others count the miracle as bestowed on Jesus or Zachariah rather than on Mary.
rows.anchor: a miracle bestowed upon Jesus or Zachariah (Ṭs) rather than upon Mary.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer repeats God’s response to Zachariah.
rows.anchor: is the same response given to Zachariah

rows.speaker: IK, R
rows.claim: Jesus demonstrates God’s creative power because he was born without a father, as Adam was created without either parent.
rows.anchor: his birth shows that God is capable of bringing a child into being without a father

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: His conception, birth, and infant speech prove his prophethood and his mother’s innocence.
rows.anchor: a sign or proof of his own prophethood and of his mother’s innocence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mary and Jesus together are called a sign, and Jesus is mercy to Mary and believers guided by him.
rows.anchor: where Mary and Jesus together are said to constitute a sign

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mary conceives when the Spirit is breathed into her; a common account says it was through her shirt opening or sleeve.
rows.anchor: according to a common account, the Spirit was breathed through the opening of her shirt or its sleeve

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus’ divine-fiat creation resembles Adam’s being given life by God’s breath, while 3:59 explicitly grounds their likeness in divine creation.
rows.anchor: Adam is similarly brought to life when God breathed into him of His Spirit

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: A report says Zachariah’s pregnant wife met Mary and the child John prostrated in the womb toward Jesus, fulfilling John’s role as confirmer.
rows.anchor: the child in the womb of Zachariah’s wife seemed to prostrate before the child in Mary’s

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some identify the distant place with the eastern area near the Temple, but the author finds more convincing a remote place where Mary was unknown.
rows.anchor: However, others describe it more convincingly as a distant place where she and her family were not known

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mary went far away to spare Zachariah embarrassment and protect herself and the child from people who might misunderstand her piety.
rows.anchor: She goes far off in order to avoid embarrassing Zachariah as well as out of fear for her child

rows.speaker: Wahb ibn Munabbih
rows.claim: Wahb reports that Mary’s relative Joseph, who served in the Temple, knew of the pregnancy and helped her.
rows.anchor: Wahb ibn Munabbih, who was familiar with the Jewish and Christian scriptures, reports that Mary’s pregnancy was known to one of her relatives named Joseph

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some accounts say Mary and Joseph later fled to Egypt as delivery approached.
rows.anchor: Some accounts assert that she later fled with Joseph to Egypt as her time of delivery drew near

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: The palm was reportedly dried, with its top cut off, and the season was winter, making fresh ripe dates miraculous.
rows.anchor: the season is said to have been winter (R, Z), making the tree’s production of ripe dates in v. 25 particularly miraculous

rows.speaker: Aj, IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: Mary’s wish to have died refers to labor pain and the shame of facing people alone with a child and no husband.
rows.anchor: the physical pain of labor and embarrassment about what people would think of her (Aj, IK, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Her longing for death need not imply lack of patience, contentment, or trust in God.
rows.anchor: should not be understood to mean that she lacked patience, contentment, or trust in God (Aj).

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says the righteous may long for death amid suffering while still fearing or grieving its consequences; he cites ʿAlī before the Camel.
rows.anchor: longing for death is often the response of the righteous to suffering (R)

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: Nasyan and mansiyyan derive from one root and express a wish to be wholly erased from memory.
rows.anchor: different forms of the same root and convey Mary’s desire to be completely forgotten from memory

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Spiritually, Mary’s statement expresses victory over ego through wanting to withdraw from and be forgotten by the world.
rows.anchor: the ultimate victory against the worldly ego

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: The speaker calling to Mary may be Gabriel or Jesus; many favor Jesus because he speaks from below after birth.
rows.anchor: many consider it more likely that it is Jesus addressing her after he has been delivered

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: If Gabriel is speaking, “from below her” may mean “in front of her.”
rows.anchor: may mean “in front of her” (Ṭ, Ṭs).

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: “From below her” may refer to the feminine palm trunk; alternatively Gabriel may call from the valley or mountain foot.
rows.anchor: from below the palm trunk (Ṭ, Z), which is also grammatically feminine

rows.speaker: IK, Qu, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Sariyyan may mean a noble or distinguished person and describe Jesus rather than a rivulet.
rows.anchor: some suggest that sariyyan, which can also be an adjective meaning “noble” or “distinguished,” may be a description of Jesus himself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dried palm produces fresh dates, paralleling John’s birth to an old barren mother and Mary’s out-of-season fruit.
rows.anchor: symbolically replicates the miracle of the birth of John from his old and formerly barren mother

rows.speaker: IK, Q, Z
rows.claim: Eating the dates nourishes Mary’s body and is said to help women during childbirth.
rows.anchor: to nourish her body with the fresh dates, said to be particularly beneficial for women during childbirth

rows.speaker: Bḍ, IK, Rb, Z
rows.claim: Eating can also nourish her soul and console her; the miraculous food and drink symbolize God’s love and concern.
rows.anchor: the provision of miraculous food and drink are symbolic of God’s love and concern for her

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qarrī ʿaynan is an Arabic expression for comfort and peace, also used for Moses’ mother when he was restored to her.
rows.anchor: a common Arabic expression meaning to be comforted and to become at peace

rows.speaker: Rb
rows.claim: One interpretation says Mary is to be at peace contemplating her son’s radiant beauty.
rows.anchor: Mary is enjoined to be at peace upon contemplating the radiant beauty of her son

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nadhartu is also used for Mary’s mother’s vow and resembles the Biblical Nazarite term for consecration and abstaining from speech except prayer.
rows.anchor: the same word used by Mary’s mother in making her vow to God regarding the child in her womb

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: Some Israelites and Jews of Mary’s time practiced a fast that included silence as well as abstention from food and drink.
rows.anchor: it was a practice among some Israelites and Jews of Mary’s time to fast by abstaining from speech as well as from food and drink

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Mary’s silence recalls Zachariah’s speechlessness and may serve as a sign; it lets Jesus defend her and spares her an argument.
rows.anchor: Her fast of silence, however, also allowed Jesus to speak on her behalf

rows.speaker: Bḍ, Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: Fariyyan describes something grave and serious as well as unprecedented.
rows.anchor: which indicates something that is serious and grave as well as unprecedented

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: “Sister of Aaron” does not mean Mary was the biological sister of Moses’ brother Aaron, which chronology rules out.
rows.anchor: not, according to commentators, meant to indicate that she was the biological sister

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: One view says Aaron was a byword for righteousness among Jews, so the title likens Mary to him.
rows.anchor: the name Aaron signified righteousness among the Jews of this time

rows.speaker: Th, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Another view says Aaron was a common Israelite name and Mary had a half-brother named Aaron.
rows.anchor: that Mary had a half brother named Aaron

rows.speaker: Bḍ, Th, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: The most widely held view makes Mary a descendant of Aaron and the title a reference to noble lineage.
rows.anchor: The most widely held view among the commentators is that Mary was a descendant of the prophet Aaron

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Mary pointed to Jesus to indicate that the people should speak to him.
rows.anchor: Mary pointed to the infant Jesus, indicating that they should speak to him (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Some take the people’s incredulous response as angry, since they first thought Mary was joking or mocking them.
rows.anchor: their response suggests a tone of anger, for they initially thought Mary’s instruction was meant mockingly or in jest

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: “Child in the cradle” may mean a child sitting in his mother’s lap.
rows.anchor: Child in the cradle here may mean a child in the mother’s lap (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: R, Q
rows.claim: Jesus’ infant speech may have been temporary; after speaking, he returned to ordinary infant incapacity.
rows.anchor: after delivering the statements recounted in vv. 30–33 Jesus returned to the ordinary state of an infant

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The miraculous speech was bestowed to clear Mary of blame or suspicion.
rows.anchor: in order to absolve his mother of any blame or suspicion (Q).

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabrisī
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabrisī notes an alternative that Jesus’ intellect was complete and he remained a prophet after infancy speech.
rows.anchor: some claimed that Jesus’ intellect was perfected and he was a prophet from this time onward

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Jesus’ first spoken words assert that he is God’s servant, a formulation Muslims use against claims of his divinity or divine sonship.
rows.anchor: the first words spoken by Jesus were an assertion of his servanthood in relation to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān also calls Muhammad God’s servant, and Islamic tradition gives both Muhammad and his father the name ʿAbd Allāh.
rows.anchor: one of the Prophet’s names, like the name of his father, was ʿAbd Allāh

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: “The Book” means the Gospel, decreed for Jesus’ future even though he is an infant.
rows.anchor: that it had been decreed that Jesus would be given the Book (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Th
rows.claim: Others say Jesus was taught Torah by inspiration in the womb or became a prophet as a child.
rows.anchor: Jesus was taught the Torah through inspiration while he was yet in the womb

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: Jesus being blessed means he brings spiritual benefit; one says he benefits followers of his religion.
rows.anchor: Jesus is a source of spiritual benefit (Ṭ, Z) for those who follow his religion (Th)

rows.speaker: Q, Qu, Ṭ
rows.claim: Jesus is described as a teacher of good, guide, defender of the oppressed, benefactor of the deprived, and enjoiner of right.
rows.anchor: a “teacher of the good” (Ṭ, Th, Z), a guide for those in error, a vindicator of the oppressed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer and almsgiving are paired as religious pillars for Muslims and also for the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: frequently mentioned together in the Quran as pillars of correct religious practice

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Zakāh can mean spiritual purification through avoiding sin and disobedience, as well as almsgiving.
rows.anchor: may also refer to the practice of purifying oneself spiritually by avoiding sin and disobedience (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “So long as I live” means Jesus’ earthly life; Muslims believe he was taken to God and will return and die before the end.
rows.anchor: Muslims believe that Jesus has not yet died; he was taken directly to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus’ filial piety parallels John’s, with Qurʾānic links on dutifulness to parents.
rows.anchor: Jesus, like John in v. 14, is characterized by filial piety

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Q
rows.claim: Jesus was neither arrogant nor disobedient, and was not violent in anger.
rows.anchor: neither arrogant nor disobedient to God’s commands (Ṭ) nor violent in anger (Q).

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: A report depicts Jesus’ humble life: mostly plant food, coarse clothing, sitting on the ground, and itinerancy.
rows.anchor: he ate mostly plant foods, wore a coarse hair shirt, sat on the ground, and was itinerant

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Th
rows.claim: When a woman praised Jesus’ mother and nursing, Jesus said the truly happy are those who recite and follow scripture.
rows.anchor: “Happy are those who recite the Book of God and follow what is in it”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A similar teaching about Jesus’ true family appears in Mark, Matthew, and Luke.
rows.anchor: A similar sentiment is conveyed in Mark 3:31–35; Matthew 12:46–50; and Luke 8:19–21

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Jesus’ threefold peace parallels John’s and means Satan did not touch him at birth.
rows.anchor: he was spared Satan’s touch on the day he was born (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Jesus will be free from fear at death after his return and at resurrection with humanity.
rows.anchor: he will be free from fear on the day he dies (after his return to earth

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: “A statement of the truth” most likely describes the Qurʾānic account of Jesus, against Jewish rejection of his prophethood and Christian divinity/sonship claims.
rows.anchor: the account of Jesus as presented in the Quran, which is understood by Muslim commentators to be the true account of his life and person

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Alternatively, the phrase may describe Jesus’ words in the preceding verses.
rows.anchor: The phrase might also be meant to describe the words uttered by Jesus in vv. 30–33

rows.speaker: Q, Th
rows.claim: Another possibility connects the phrase to Jesus as God’s Word in 3:45, though the wording differs.
rows.anchor: a statement of the truth may be related to the description of Jesus as a Word from God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because al-Ḥaqq is a divine name, “a statement of the truth” may mean “the Word of God.”
rows.anchor: Truth here to be a reference to God, so that a statement of the truth could be rendered “the Word of God”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān repeatedly rejects the claim that God has a child and pairs such denials with glorification.
rows.anchor: The Quran repeatedly rejects and derides the notion that God could have a child

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse’s creative “Be” fiat echoes other passages and is applied specifically to Jesus in 3:59.
rows.anchor: Regarding the Divine creative fiat Be! as the means by which God brings creatures into existence

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: The verse may continue Jesus’ speech, as translated; its first sentence closely matches his words in 5:117.
rows.anchor: this verse is read as a continuation of the words that Jesus speaks in vv. 30–33

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On that reading, Jesus reiterates his servanthood, and worship is directed to God, Jesus’ Lord as well as theirs.
rows.anchor: those who would worship Jesus should worship God instead

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: Alternatively, the verse may continue 19:34: “That is Jesus son of Mary … and that is God, my Lord and your Lord.”
rows.anchor: the verse may also be read as a continuation from v. 34

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The straight path is true religion leading to salvation.
rows.anchor: understood to be the path of true religion that leads to salvation

rows.speaker: Q, Z
rows.claim: The parties may mean Jews and Christians, who disagree about Jesus’ status.
rows.anchor: the Jews and the Christians, who differ with each other over the status of Jesus

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Alternatively, the parties may be Christian sects such as Jacobites and Nestorians.
rows.anchor: different Christian sects, for example, the Jacobites and Nestorians

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: Witnessing the great day may mean experiencing the fear of reckoning and punishment on Resurrection Day.
rows.anchor: great fear in the face of the reckoning and punishment meted out on the Day of Resurrection

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Witnessing may mean testimony against disbelievers by angels, prophets, religious leaders, and their own limbs.
rows.anchor: the testimony of the angels, the prophets, and leaders of their respective religious communities

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Mashhad literally denotes the time and place of judgment, whose scene induces great fear.
rows.anchor: most literally denotes the time and place of the reckoning and judgment

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: On Judgment Day disbelievers hear and see keenly, unlike their worldly spiritual deafness and blindness to revelation.
rows.anchor: in contrast to their spiritual “blindness” and “deafness” in earthly life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Last Day removes the cover and makes sight piercing; another image says the spiritually blind are raised blind.
rows.anchor: Now We have removed from you your cover; so today your sight is piercing

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: Their keen perception on that day cannot benefit them, just as last-minute belief cannot benefit those who disbelieved in life.
rows.anchor: it will be of no benefit to them, just as believing on this Day brings no benefit to those who were not believers in earthly life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is told to warn Quraysh of the Day of Regret, a name found only here, though regret over evil deeds appears elsewhere.
rows.anchor: the Prophet is instructed to warn the Quraysh of the Day of Regret

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Some say the damned first see the Garden homes prepared for them had they believed, intensifying regret.
rows.anchor: those whose disbelief and evil deeds earned them a place in Hellfire will first be shown the dwellings in the Garden

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The matter is decreed” marks final judgment, after which repentance cannot change one’s eternal fate.
rows.anchor: after the coming of the Last Day, one no longer has the opportunity to repent and mend one’s ways

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: A ḥadīth says death is brought as a ram and slaughtered before Garden and Fire dwellers, showing their fates cannot change.
rows.anchor: God will bring forth death itself in the form of a ram and “slaughter” it
